content.text: Browsers attach your site's cookies to requests that other sites start, so a valid session cookie proves which browser sent a request, not which page. That's cross-site request forgery (CSRF). SameSite cookies narrow the gap but don't close it. Never change state on GET, and require proof that the other site can't produce: a CSRF token, ideally from your framework.
A user reports that two-factor authentication on her account was switched off, and she didn't do it. The logs show

from her own browser, with her valid session cookie, so the first reply from the team is that she must have clicked it herself. She did click something: a link in a forum post, a few seconds earlier. The page behind it navigated her browser to that URL, and her browser added the cookie, as browsers do.

The belief: a request that carries the user's session cookie must have come from your own site. Only your site set the cookie, and other sites can't read it, so the cookie proves the user acted in your app.
The first half is true, which is why the belief holds. The
does stop other sites from reading your cookies and your responses. Session cookies are usually scoped to your domain, marked
, and sent only over HTTPS. Chromium-based browsers treat cookies without a SameSite attribute as

, which many developers remember as "cross-site requests don't get cookies". But reading a cookie and sending one are different things. The attacker never needs to read it. The browser attaches it for them.
The browser attaches cookies, not your page

OWASP's CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet starts from the mechanism: "browser requests automatically include all cookies including session cookies." Microsoft's docs say the same: these attacks "are possible because web browsers send some types of authentication tokens automatically with every request to a website." The cookie identifies the browser. It says nothing about which page, tab or site started the request. So, in OWASP's words, "unprotected target sites cannot distinguish between legitimate authorized requests and forged authenticated requests."
Another site can send even when it can't read
MDN explains why forms are the classic tool: "Simple requests, which are the sort of request that result from a

element submission, can be made cross-origin without being blocked." The other site never sees your response, and it doesn't need to: the email is changed, the money is sent, 2FA is off. MDN lists when an app is exposed: it changes state with HTTP requests, it "Uses only cookies to validate that the request came from an authenticated user", and every parameter is predictable. The OWASP Top 10 2025 lists CSRF, CWE-352, among the notable weaknesses of A01 Broken Access Control.
SameSite narrows the gap, but it isn't the wall
attribute tells the browser when to withhold a cookie from cross-site requests. ASP.NET Core's cookie authentication defaults to
. We tested the three values in headless Chromium 156, with a page on one local site sending requests to an app on another:

blocks.code: Cookie Request started by the other site Cookie sent SameSite=None auto-submitted POST form yes SameSite=Lax auto-submitted POST form no SameSite=Lax auto-submitted GET form (navigates) yes SameSite=Lax pointing at the GET URL no SameSite=Strict any of the three no

content.text: That third line is the story above. OWASP calls it "the single most common way SameSite-based defenses fail in practice": "If any state-changing operation in the application is reachable via a GET request, SameSite=Lax will not stop it." There are other gaps. SameSite works per site, not per origin, so MDN warns that "you have to trust all your site's subdomains." And defaults differ: "Chromium-based browsers treat cookies without a SameSite attribute as Lax, but Firefox and Safari do not."
What proves intent: something the other site can't produce

token is a random value the server puts in its own page and checks on every state-changing request. As MDN puts it, "Because an attacker can't guess the token value, they can't issue a successful forgery." Browsers also help: in our test, every forged request arrived with
, a header page scripts can't set, so a server can refuse cross-site writes. APIs called with
can require a custom header or a JSON body, which turns the call into a request the browser won't send cross-origin without permission.
Moving the action behind a token

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The fix doesn't invent anything. OWASP's first rule is "check if your framework has built-in CSRF protection and use it", and Microsoft documents that "By default, Minimal APIs that accept form data require antiforgery token validation and fail before running application code if antiforgery validation isn't successful." A forged form has no valid token, so the handler never runs. Asking for the password again follows OWASP's advice to consider "user interaction based protection for highly sensitive operations."

content.text: OWASP is blunt: "Remember that Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) can defeat all CSRF mitigation techniques!" Script running in your own page can read the token and send a same-origin request. CSRF protection assumes your output encoding holds.

blocks.title: Hunt for state changes on GET

content.text: actions that save, delete, send or toggle anything. Each one is open to a plain link, whatever your SameSite setting. Move them to POST, PUT or DELETE.
CSRF needs credentials the browser sends by itself: cookies, and, as Microsoft notes, Basic and Digest authentication. An API that only accepts a bearer token in the
header is not exposed this way, because no browser adds that header on its own.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: List the state-changing endpoints that use cookies

content.text: Every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, plus any GET that writes, where the user is identified by a cookie.
Move every action that changes state off GET. That alone closes the gap
for Minimal APIs; MVC and Razor Pages validate tokens through built-in filters. Never answer a failing token with
for session cookies when your login flow allows it, otherwise
. Treat it as defense in depth.
Changing the email or password, disabling 2FA and sending money should ask for the password or a second factor again.

items.text: A session cookie proves which browser sent a request, not which site started it.
Other sites can't read your cookies, but they can make the browser send them.
blocks cross-site POSTs in Chromium, yet it lets top-level GET navigations through.
Use your framework's CSRF tokens on every state-changing request, and keep GET read-only.
XSS defeats CSRF defenses, so CSRF protection only works on top of solid output encoding.
